title: LGM-1, the 'little green men' star
hook: The first pulsar ticked so steadily that its finders nicknamed it Little Green Men.
peek: In 1967 a Cambridge graduate student spotted a strange smudge on her chart paper. It pulsed every 1.3 seconds, as regular as a clock, and for a few weeks nobody could rule out that someone out there was signalling.
lede: In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a graduate student at Cambridge, was checking long rolls of chart paper from a new radio telescope when she noticed a small patch of what she called scruff. Looked at closely, it was a string of pulses arriving every 1.3 seconds with clockwork precision. Nothing natural was known to tick like that, so the team half-jokingly labelled it LGM-1, for Little Green Men.

bullets.text: Just before Christmas 1967, Bell found another pulsing source in a different part of the sky. Two separate alien groups signalling in the same odd way seemed very unlikely, so the Little Green Men idea was quietly dropped.
Pulsars turned out to be neutron stars, the collapsed cores of big stars, spinning and sweeping a radio beam past Earth like a lighthouse. LGM-1 is now catalogued as PSR B1919+21.

The stacked wavy lines on Joy Division's 1979 album Unknown Pleasures are a chart of this same pulsar's pulses. The image came from a 1970 astronomy thesis and was reprinted in an encyclopedia of astronomy, where the band found it.

The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for pulsars went to her supervisor Antony Hewish and to Martin Ryle, not to Bell, which many astronomers questioned. In 2018 she won a $3 million Breakthrough Prize and gave it all to fund physics students.
